title: Statement of Retraction: Study on the role and mechanism of lncRNA in the remodeling of atrial energy metabolism in rabbits with atrial fibrillation based on nano sensor technology.
Time to Storm the Next CASTLE: Can Atrial Fibrillation Ablation Improve Outcomes in Patients With Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction?
summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and atrial fibrillation frequently coexist and are linked by shared mechanisms including atrial myopathy, elevated filling pressures, fibrosis, and adverse hemodynamic interactions. The combination of both diseases worsens patient outcomes, and catheter ablation has emerged as a potentially important treatment strategy in this population. This review aims to summarize and highlight the current evidence on ablation in patients with atrial fibrillation and HFpEF.

RECENT FINDINGS: When examining outcomes of mortality, hospitalization, hemodynamics, and recurrence, ablation appears to be superior to medical treatment with some mixed results. However, no large trials have been conducted on the topic, and no clear guidelines for ablation in HFpEF patients exist. Ablation is promising but not yet definitive for patients with atrial fibrillation and HFpEF. Ongoing trials, including CASTLE-HFpEF should clarify the gaps including patient selection, procedural strategy, and outcome benefit.

title: Atrial Fibrillation Across the Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation Continuum: A Systematic Scoping Evidence Map.
summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (AF/AFL) are clinically relevant complications across the haematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) continuum, but evidence supporting phase-specific management and transitions of care remains fragmented. This review aimed to map direct HCT-AF evidence, broader HCT cardiovascular evidence, and relevant guidance; identify major evidence-to-care gaps; and define an evidence-informed framework for AF/AFL management across the HCT continuum.

RECENT FINDINGS: We conducted a systematic scoping evidence map of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, supplemented by a predefined closed hand-search of guidance sources. Twenty-seven clinical reports and 15 guidance documents were retained, yielding 42 evidence sources. Direct evidence was concentrated on AF/AFL incidence, timing, predictors, recurrence, and prognosis, whereas evidence for treatment selection, rhythm-surveillance strategies, anticoagulation during thrombocytopenia, and survivorship follow-up remained limited and frequently dependent on extrapolated guidance. The evidence map informed a phase-specific care framework spanning pre-HCT risk assessment, risk-adapted rhythm surveillance, structured acute AF/AFL assessment, dynamic anticoagulation reassessment, medication-safety review, and accountable discharge and survivorship follow-up. AF/AFL after HCT should be viewed as a longitudinal care challenge rather than an isolated inpatient arrhythmic event. The proposed phase-specific quality-of-care processes are hypothesis-generating and require prospective evaluation for feasibility, reproducibility, implementation, and association with clinical outcomes.

title: Controversy: Atrial fibrillation ablation should be performed in patients with HFpEF
summary: Abstract The role of atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation in the management of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains an under investigated issue with no robust clinical trials data. This controversy reviews the evidence for and against AF ablation in this complex condition from two different perspectives reviewing mechanistic and observational evidence aswell as proposing future directions for research in the field.

title: Association of coffee and tea consumption with the risk of atrial fibrillation: a prospective cohort study from the UK Biobank.
summary:
OBJECTIVES: Atrial fibrillation (AF) has a high prevalence and a heavy healthcare burden, making prevention of AF essential. Coffee and tea are popular beverages around the world, and they may have a relationship with AF, but the results are controversial. This study aimed to investigate the relationship of coffee and tea intake with the risk of AF.

METHODS: This study included 495,269 participants without AF at baseline from the UK Biobank. Coffee and tea intake was self-reported (0, 0.5-1, 2-3, ≥ 4 cups/day). Cox regression was used to estimate hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals.

RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 13.04 ± 2.26 years, 37,261 participants developed AF. The associations of coffee and tea with AF were non-linear (P for non-linear < 0.001). Compared with non-drinkers, drinking 0.5-1, 2-3, and ≥ 4 cups of coffee per day was associated with a protective effect against AF, corresponding to a 7, 11, and 9% lower risk, respectively. For tea, only consumption of 2-3 cups per day was associated with a modestly lower risk of AF, whereas no significant associations were observed for other intake categories.

CONCLUSIONS: We found that coffee intake was inversely associated with incident AF across multiple intake categories, whereas for tea, a modest inverse association was observed only at 2-3 cups per day, with no statistically significant associations for other intake categories. Further studies are warranted to confirm our findings and clarify the potential mechanism.

title: Which score best predicts new-onset AF after primary PCI in STEMI? Head-to-head assessment of four algorithms.
summary:
BACKGROUND: New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) is a frequent and clinically significant comorbidity following primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), associated with increased mortality, stroke risk, and healthcare costs. Predicting NOAF in this setting remains challenging. This study aimed to compare the predictive performance of four risk scores-CHA2DS2-VASc-60, mC2HEST, Mayo-AF, and HATCH-in identifying patients at high risk of NOAF after primary PCI in STEMI.

METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study at Shaoxing Central Hospital, including consecutive adults with STEMI who underwent primary PCI within 12 h of symptom onset between February 2020 and June 2025. Patients with a history of atrial fibrillation or other exclusions were excluded. The endpoint was NOAF within 1 year after PCI, documented by continuous inpatient telemetry, 12-lead ECG at discharge, and routine follow-up ECGs at 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. We compared the discriminative ability of the four scores using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and assessed their clinical utility through net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).

RESULTS: A total of 1,175 patients were included in the final analysis. The incidence of NOAF within 1 year was 8.2% (n = 96). The mC2HEST score demonstrated the highest area under the ROC curve (AUC) for predicting NOAF (AUC = 0.786), followed by HATCH (AUC = 0.746) and CHA2DS2-VASc-60 (AUC = 0.739), while Mayo-AF had the lowest AUC (AUC = 0.736).Pairwise comparisons showed that mC2HEST significantly outperformed CHA2DS2-VASc-60 (ΔAUC = 0.046, p = 0.002).

CONCLUSIONS: Among the four risk scores evaluated, mC2HEST provided the best predictive performance for NOAF after primary PCI in STEMI patients. Its superior discriminative ability and significant integrated discrimination improvement suggest that mC2HEST could be a valuable tool for identifying high-risk patients who may benefit from intensified monitoring and early interventions. Future prospective, multicenter studies are warranted to validate these findings.

title: Reversible heart failure and subsequent bradyarrhythmia during long-term follow-up in a patient with chronic hypocalcemia: a case report.
summary: Chronic hypocalcemia is an uncommon, potentially reversible cause of heart failure. Existing reports have mainly described recovery of ventricular function with calcium correction, whereas long-term rhythm outcomes after clinical improvement remain poorly characterized. We report the case of a 74-year-old man with a history of hypocalcemia for more than 40 years and coronary artery disease for 19 years, who was admitted for acute decompensated heart failure. He was ultimately diagnosed with hypocalcemic cardiomyopathy. Following calcium and calcitriol supplementation together with heart failure therapy, his dyspnea resolved, the corrected QT interval shortened, and echocardiography demonstrated improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction. However, 11 months after discharge, he developed persistent atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response and intermittent third-degree atrioventricular block, subsequently underwent permanent pacemaker implantation after clinical evaluation. This case highlights the importance of long-term rhythm surveillance after recovery from hypocalcemic cardiomyopathy, while recognizing that late arrhythmic events may be influenced by multiple contributing factors.

title: Impact of low-voltage area burden and topological obstacles on atrial fibrillation recurrence after pulmonary vein antrum isolation.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Topological obstacles (TOs), electrically isolated regions such as the mitral annulus and atrial scars, can provide reentry circuits in the left atrium. Their quantity and relationship with low-voltage area (LVA) burden may influence recurrent atrial fibrillation (AF), but this impact remains poorly understood. We aimed to investigate the association between TO count, LVA burden, and post-ablation AF recurrence in patients undergoing de novo AF ablation.

METHODS: Patients were categorized by TO counts, identified using pulmonary vein antrum isolation lines and voltage maps. LVA burden (<0.5 mV) was quantified and grouped into quartiles. One-year AF/atrial tachycardia (AT) recurrence was evaluated across groups.

RESULTS: Among 237 patients (mean age 62.4 ± 8.8 years; 27.0% female, paroxysmal AF 42.6%, follow-up 1.0 ± 0. years), the majority had an intermediate TO count (TO = 3, 75.9%). Patients with the lowest TO count (TO = 1, 5.5%) were significantly older, had higher CHA2DS2-VASc scores, worse echocardiographic parameters, and the highest mean LVA burden (36.6% ± 24.8%). AF/AT recurrence occurred in 35.4% of patients. Although recurrence rates were numerically higher in patients with extreme TO counts (TO = 1 or ≥4) and lower in those with intermediate counts (TO = 2 or 3), these differences were not statistically significant (p = 0.433), and the TO group remained non-significantly associated with recurrence after multivariable adjustment for age, AF clinical type, left atrial diameter, left ventricular ejection fraction, CHA2DS2-VASc score, and LVA burden. TO counts differed significantly across LVA burden quartiles (p < 0.001), with the greatest variation observed in the group with the highest LVA burden. Dominant frequency and organization index showed no significant intergroup differences.

CONCLUSION: Patients with extreme TO counts (TO = 1 or ≥4) showed a numerically higher, although not statistically significant, trend toward post-ablation recurrence compared with those with intermediate counts. TO quantity varied significantly with LVA burden, suggesting that atrial substrate heterogeneity may influence AF recurrence patterns.

title: Feasibility of steerable sheath-guided left atrial appendage closure in challenging anatomy.
summary:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an established treatment option for stroke prevention in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) who are unsuitable for long-term oral anticoagulation. However, an anatomically challenging left atrial appendage (LAA) can limit optimal device positioning and complete occlusion with conventional fixed-curve sheaths.Two elderly men with NVAF and high bleeding risk underwent LAAC using Watchman FLX Pro devices (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA). Pre-procedural imaging revealed anatomically challenging LAAs. With a standard double-curve sheath, one case showed unacceptable posterior protrusion of a large 40-mm device. In another case, tilting of the device led to incomplete coverage of the posterior lobe, resulting in a residual peri-device leak. After switching to the TruSteer™ Access System (Boston Scientific), a bidirectional steerable sheath, improved coaxial alignment, enabled acceptable device protrusion, complete sealing with no residual leak, and stable device release in both cases. These cases suggest that a steerable sheath can overcome the limitations of fixed-curve sheaths in anatomically challenging LAAs by enabling coaxial alignment and optimized posterior wall apposition during LAAC.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE: In wide-neck, shallow, or multilobed left atrial appendages (LAAs), failure to meet PASS criteria with a conventional fixed-curve sheath may reflect non-coaxial deployment and, with very large devices, sheath instability due to kick-back at release, leading to device tilt. A bidirectional steerable sheath provides real-time control of the delivery axis and may prevent kick-back at release, enabling reproducible optimal device positioning in anatomically challenging LAAs where fixed-curve sheaths are inadequate.

title: Atrial leadless pacing for heart failure in sick sinus syndrome.
summary:
Two patients with sick sinus syndrome and heart failure were treated with atrial leadless pacing. Case 1 demonstrated hemodynamic improvement with cardiac output increase (3.0 → 5.1 L/min), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) reduction (3223 → 480 pg/mL), and New York Heart Association class improvement (III → I) following Aveir dual-chamber leadless pacemaker (Abbott Medical, Inc., Plymouth, MN, USA) implantation. Case 2, at high infection risk with mechanical valve and prior endocarditis, received hybrid therapy combining atrial fibrillation ablation, Aveir atrial pacing, and subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation, achieving left ventricular ejection fraction improvement (20 → 38%) and BNP reduction (321 → 28 pg/mL). Atrial leadless pacing may represent a therapeutic option in selected patients with preserved atrioventricular conduction or high infection risk requiring physiologic pacing.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE: This case report demonstrates that atrial leadless pacing can be an effective treatment option for patients with sick sinus syndrome complicated by heart failure when conventional transvenous atrial pacing is undesirable. In one of the presented cases, the feasibility of combining a leadless pacemaker with a subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is also illustrated, providing insight into a potential lead-free device strategy.

title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.

OBJECTIVE: This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.

METHODS: The prompt "Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient" was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

RESULTS: The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).

CONCLUSIONS: The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.

title: Vascular Mania in Late Life: Acute Pontine Infarction, Autoimmune Hyperthyroidism, and Atrial Fibrillation Converging in a 61-Year-Old Man.
Outpatient Initiation of Sotalol: Reappraising Risk, Monitoring, and Modern Care Pathways.
summary: Sotalol remains an important antiarrhythmic drug for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation and other supraventricular arrhythmias. However, sotalol is traditionally initiated in the inpatient setting because of concerns regarding QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. This practice is based on early observational data collected before the availability of contemporary risk stratification, standardized protocols, and modern rhythm monitoring technologies. Over the past two decades, evidence from observational studies using device-based monitoring, protocolized outpatient clinics, and remote electrocardiographic technologies has demonstrated low rates of malignant ventricular arrhythmias in carefully selected patients. These data also highlight the importance of longitudinal surveillance, as clinically relevant QT prolongation may occur beyond the conventional inpatient monitoring window. Thus, this review examines the pharmacologic basis of sotalol-related proarrhythmia, critically reassesses the rationale for inpatient initiation, synthesizes contemporary evidence supporting outpatient strategies in carefully selected patients with protocolized monitoring, and proposes a practical, risk-stratified framework for outpatient sotalol initiation while identifying key knowledge gaps that still require prospective validation.

title: Long-Term Survival and Predictive Relevance of Nocturnal Ventricular Tachyarrhythmias Requiring Appropriate Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Therapy.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Whether nocturnal ventricular tachyarrhythmias (VTAs) are associated with poorer long-term survival than daytime VTAs remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between nocturnal VTAs and long-term survival, as well as the associated prognostic relevance.

METHODS: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) recipients from the Study of Home Monitoring System Safety and Efficacy in Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device-implanted Patients (SUMMIT) registry were retrospectively analyzed using data from home monitoring transmissions. Nocturnal VTAs were defined as episodes occurring between 22:00 and 05:59, whereas daytime VTAs were defined as those occurring during the remaining 16 hours (06:00-21:59).

RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 61.7 months, 102 cardiac deaths and 187 deaths from any cause were recorded. Among 730 patients, 422 experienced VTAs, of whom 231 (54.7%) had nocturnal VTAs. Compared with patients without VTAs, those with nocturnal VTAs had a 62% higher risk of cardiac death (hazard ratio (HR), 1.62; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.02-2.59; p = 0.041) and a 2.3-fold higher risk of all-cause mortality (HR, 2.30; 95% CI: 1.50-3.53; p < 0.001). Patients with nocturnal VTAs experienced more ICD shocks (77.9% [180/231] vs. 59.2% [113/191]; p < 0.001), more electrical storms (46.8% [108/231] vs. 9.4% [18/191]; p < 0.001), and a higher VTA burden (median, 1.36 [IQR, 3.44] vs. 0.59 [IQR, 1.01] episodes per year) than those with daytime-only VTAs. Elevated nighttime heart rate and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), as well as male sex and prior atrial fibrillation, were identified as independent risk factors for nocturnal VTAs.

CONCLUSIONS: Nocturnal VTAs were not uncommon. Patients experiencing nocturnal VTAs had a higher risk of cardiac death and all-cause mortality. Monitoring the occurrence and timing of VTA episodes may be a useful tool for identifying high-risk patients.

title: Do We Still Need Conventional Holter ECGs in the Era of Smart Devices?
summary: Wearable devices for rhythm monitoring are increasingly available and are being used by patients across a broad spectrum of technologies, including smartwatches with electrocardiogram (ECG)-recording functions and ECG patch systems. Early development of automated rhythm classification algorithms using artificial intelligence primarily focused on atrial fibrillation (AF), although indications and validated use cases differ substantially between device types and continue to evolve. This review aims to provide an overview of contemporary smart devices, their capabilities in arrhythmia care, and future perspectives. Currently, two main technologies are used for rhythm assessment: photoplethysmography (PPG) and single- or multi-lead electrocardiography. PPG enables continuous monitoring of heart rate and pulse regularity, whereas ECG acquisition is typically user-initiated. The use of a 30-second single-lead ECG (SL-ECG) strip with physician confirmation for the diagnosis of AF is supported by current ESC AF guidelines. Systematic screening approaches using wearables have demonstrated higher AF detection rates compared with standard diagnostic pathways; however, whether this translates into improved stroke prevention remains to be proven. Beyond AF, wearables may be particularly useful for infrequent symptomatic arrhythmias, such as supraventricular tachycardias, by enabling SL-ECG recording during symptoms and thereby supporting diagnosis and management. Additional applications include monitoring of QT prolongation, conduction disturbances, and rhythm surveillance following interventions. As an established alternative to user-dependent ECG acquisition, ECG patches provide continuous rhythm recording for up to 30 days and are generally more user-friendly than conventional Holter monitoring. A key challenge remains automated rhythm detection for non-AF arrhythmias, as well as a relevant proportion of inconclusive tracings in real-world populations, for example in the presence of conduction abnormalities or frequent premature atrial or ventricular complexes. From a physician's perspective, clear workflows and dedicated technical solutions are essential to manage the growing volume of data, and reimbursement mechanisms for analysis of these recordings must be established. Ultimately, the future of wearable-based rhythm monitoring lies in its structured integration into clinical workflows, enabling more individualized and optimized arrhythmia care. In parallel, combining rhythm information with additional health metrics may facilitate a more holistic approach to prevention and management of cardiovascular disease. Despite all technical advances, traditional Holter ECG still has irreplaceable value in patients with frequent arrhythmia symptoms or when coronary vasospasms or Brugada syndrome are suspected.

title: Stage-dependent predictors of atrial fibrillation recurrence after catheter ablation: a proof-of-concept analysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Risk models for atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence after catheter ablation apply the same predictor structure to every patient. This overlooks the biological differences between early and advanced disease. We examined whether the clinical predictors of 12-month recurrence differ across four disease-stage phenotypes.

METHODS: This retrospective cohort study enrolled 419 consecutive patients who underwent first-time radiofrequency ablation at Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, between October 2021 and June 2024. The institutional protocol was pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) alone, and patients undergoing concurrent left atrial appendage occlusion were excluded. Patients were classified by AF type and duration into four groups: early paroxysmal (Phenotype 1, ≤ 12 months, n = 225), long-standing paroxysmal (Phenotype 2, > 12 months, n = 86), recent-onset persistent (Phenotype 3, ≤ 18 months, n = 62), and long-duration persistent AF (Phenotype 4, > 18 months, n = 46). We performed phenotype-specific logistic regression, predictor × phenotype interaction testing, Kaplan-Meier and restricted mean survival analysis, and ROC analysis.

RESULTS: Twelve-month recurrence occurred in 88 patients (21.0%) and differed significantly across phenotypes (17.3%, 20.9%, 16.1%, and 45.7% in P1-P4; p < 0.001). Recurrence-free survival was worst in P4 (log-rank p < 0.001). In the overall model (AUC 0.672), the independent predictors were persistent AF type, longer duration, and hypertension, the last associated with lower recurrence. Phenotype-specific models revealed distinct profiles, and the sex × phenotype interaction was formally significant (p = 0.0042). In P1, younger age was the only predictor (AUC 0.701). In P3, female sex and hypertension were apparent predictors (apparent AUC 0.862; recurrence 43.8% in women vs. 6.5% in men), although this estimate is subject to optimism given only 10 events. In P4, no clinical variable was associated with recurrence despite its 45.7% rate, though power was insufficient to exclude moderate associations. The protective direction of hypertension strengthened across P1-P3 before disappearing in P4.

CONCLUSION: In this exploratory, single-center analysis, the clinical predictors of post-ablation AF recurrence appeared to shift across the four disease-stage phenotypes, with formal statistical support for sex. We propose the Predictor Lifecycle as a testable hypothesis for prospective, multicenter validation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not constitute a validated risk-stratification framework for clinical use.

title: Antidiabetic Therapy and Atrial Fibrillation: Pathophysiological Links, Therapeutic Implications, and Evidence-Based Outcomes.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is strongly associated with an increased risk, severity, and recurrence of Atrial Fibrillation (AF). This narrative review aims to synthesize the mechanistic links between DM and AF and evaluate the impact of major antidiabetic drug categories on AF incidence, burden, and post-ablation outcomes.

METHODS: A focused narrative review of the literature was conducted using predefined eligibility criteria for study selection and specific keywords to search major scientific databases and grey literature.

RESULTS: Hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, epicardial adipose tissue expansion, autonomic imbalance, and atrial remodeling represent core pathophysiological mechanisms connecting DM and AF. Among antidiabetic pharmacotherapies, the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide displays a potential to reduce AF incidence. Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors have similarly been shown to lower the incidence of AF in most of the available evidence, while offering an emerging, preliminary benefit for post-ablation success. Metformin also demonstrates a positive impact across both primary and secondary AF prevention, albeit with less robust evidence. Other incretin therapies, including tirzepatide, exhibit neutral effects, while thiazolidinediones and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors yield conflicting results. Data from insulin and sulfonylureas suggest an unfavorable risk profile, though potentially confounded by indication.

DISCUSSION: Antidiabetic therapy selection may have clinically meaningful implications for AF risk modification and rhythm-control outcomes. Weight-centric and cardio-protective strategies, particularly SGLT2 inhibitors and semaglutide, alongside the traditional option of metformin, show promising signals. Nevertheless, available data derive largely from unadjudicated adverseevent reporting and observational cohorts, currently precluding definitive class-wide or agentspecific recommendations.

CONCLUSION: Incorporating atrial fibrillation risk into the individualization of antidiabetic therapy is a promising and clinically relevant strategy. However, establishing any specific agent as a preferred option for AF management remains premature in the absence of dedicated trials with primary AF endpoints.

title: Pacing Performance of a Modular Communicative Leadless Pacing-Defibrillator System
summary: Abstract Background and Aims MODULAR ATP is an ongoing trial assessing the efficacy of a subcutaneous implantable cardioverter defibrillator (S-ICD) in communication with a leadless pacemaker (LP) that can deliver bradycardia pacing and antitachycardia pacing. The objective of this study was to assess safety and pacing performance of the investigational LP. Methods The study enrolled patients with an ICD indication and at high risk for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Pacemaker dependent patients were excluded. Primary safety endpoint 2 was the percentage of patients free from major LP-related complications at 12 months. The secondary effectiveness endpoint assessed the rate response performance of the LP under workload. Parameters related to the pacing performance were also measured. Results In 297 patients, the mean age was 59±12 years, the mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 35.3±13.1%, and 17.5% were female. LP implant was attempted in 286 patients and was successful in 100%. The major LP-related complication free rate at 12 months was 97.2% (one-sided 97.5% LCL 94.5%), surpassing the performance goal of 81%. There were no LP-related complications following Implant. For the secondary effectiveness endpoint, the slope of the normalized sensor rate versus the normalized workload was 0.96 (95% LCL 0.91, 95% UCL 1.02), within the performance goal range of 0.65-1.35. At 12 months, 96.8% of patients had a pacing capture threshold ≤ 2V @ 0.4ms pulse width. Conclusions The performance of the modular pacing-defibrillator system at one year demonstrated a low complication rate and reliable pacing functionality.

title: Intramyocardial Granulomatous Histoplasmosis Presenting as Narrow-Complex Ventricular Tachycardia.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Cardiac histoplasmosis is rare, typically manifesting as pericarditis or endocarditis; tissue-proven intramyocardial granulomatous histoplasmosis has not been previously described.

CASE SUMMARY: A 77-year-old man with immunosuppression presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and recurrent narrow-complex tachyarrhythmias attributed to supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Echocardiography showed a hyperechoic basal septal mass. Autopsy confirmed a 1.8 × 1.1 cm partially hyalinized necrotizing granuloma of the high interventricular septum containing Histoplasma on silver staining. Retrospective aVR algorithm analysis reclassified the arrhythmia as ventricular tachycardia (VT), anatomically concordant with the granuloma.

DISCUSSION: Granulomatous histoplasmosis of the upper interventricular septum can produce high septal VT mimicking SVT, expanding the differential of granulomatous myocarditis in immunocompromised hosts.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Histoplasmosis should be included in the differential of granulomatous myocarditis, particularly in immunocompromised patients from endemic regions. Systematic use of the Vereckei aVR algorithm can prevent misclassification of relatively narrow-complex VT as SVT and guide management.

title: Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia With Propofol Infusion Syndrome in Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) is a rare, potentially fatal complication of prolonged or high-dose propofol exposure characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic derangements, and cardiovascular collapse. The classically described mode of cardiac death is bradycardia progressing to asystole.

CASE SUMMARY: A previously healthy 21-year-old woman presented 5 days after a vaginal delivery with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring sedation with propofol escalated to 100 μg/kg/min. She developed rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and progressive ventricular ectopy that evolved into pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Propofol was stopped, and continuous renal replacement therapy was arranged, but the patient experienced cardiac arrest before initiation. No arrhythmias occurred after metabolic correction.

DISCUSSION: This case highlights pulseless ventricular tachycardia as a rare cardiac manifestation of PRIS with evolving metabolic abnormalities before cardiovascular collapse occurs.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia during prolonged propofol therapy should prompt evaluation for PRIS. Early propofol discontinuation and aggressive metabolic correction may prevent fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

title: Efficacy of Quinidine in Brugada Syndrome: A Literature Review.
summary: Brugada syndrome (BrS) is an inherited arrhythmogenic disorder associated with an increased risk of ventricular fibrillation (VF) and sudden cardiac death. Quinidine and hydroquinidine are currently used to prevent ventricular arrhythmias in BrS. This review summarizes the available evidence on the efficacy, safety, and clinical applications of these drugs in BrS. Ten studies involving more than 300 patients with BrS were analyzed. Quinidine or hydroquinidine therapy prevented VF inducibility in 42.9-90% of cases and reduced recurrent arrhythmic events by approximately 60-70%. Among patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs), reductions in both appropriate and inappropriate shock counts were observed. Gastrointestinal intolerance was the most common side effect, occurring in 20-30% of patients, with drug discontinuation in up to 26%. QT prolongation was infrequent, and serious proarrhythmic events were rare. Despite these benefits, quinidine remains unavailable or difficult to access in many regions, limiting its widespread clinical use. In conclusion, quinidine and hydroquinidine exert antiarrhythmic effects in BrS and reduce the recurrence of ventricular arrhythmias, particularly among ICD-treated or high-risk patients. Although therapy is constrained by gastrointestinal intolerance and limited availability, low-dose regimens may be better tolerated while maintaining efficacy. These agents can be considered, in selected patients, as adjuncts or alternatives to device therapy; meanwhile, further multicenter studies are warranted to confirm long-term safety, determine optimal dosing, and improve global accessibility.

title: Cardiovascular effects of methylphenidate, risperidone, and their combination in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a prospective 3-month observational study.
summary:
BACKGROUND: We aimed to evaluate changes in hemodynamic parameters and electrocardiographic (ECG) indices related to ventricular arrhythmia risk after three months of treatment with methylphenidate (MPH), risperidone (RIS), or their combination in children and adolescents with ADHD.

METHODS: A total of 150 children and adolescents with DSM-5-diagnosed ADHD were prospectively enrolled at Qods Hospital. Participants received methylphenidate (n = 50), risperidone (n = 50), or combination therapy (n = 50). Cardiovascular outcomes were assessed using age- and weight-adjusted two-way repeated-measures ANCOVA to evaluate changes over time and differences among treatment groups.

RESULTS: Significant group × time interactions were observed for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, and QTc interval after adjustment for baseline age and weight. After three months, systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased in the methylphenidate and combination therapy groups, while heart rate showed an overall increase, with the greatest rise observed in the methylphenidate group. QTc interval increased over time across all treatment groups, with the largest prolongation observed in the combination therapy group (377.9 ± 25.4 to 424.5 ± 24.9 ms). However, mean QTc values remained below commonly accepted thresholds for clinically significant QT prolongation, and no significant longitudinal changes were observed in QRS duration or PR intervals.

CONCLUSION: Treatment with methylphenidate, risperidone, and combination therapy was associated with modest changes in heart rate, blood pressure, and QTc interval over three months. These findings highlight the importance of baseline and follow-up cardiovascular monitoring in children and adolescents receiving ADHD medications.

title: Repolarization Heterogeneity and Ventricular Arrhythmias in Ischemia- Reperfusion.
summary: Augmented spatial heterogeneity of ventricular repolarization is considered to constitute an arrhythmogenic substrate that predisposes to malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Since acute myocardial infarction is inherently accompanied by increased repolarization dispersion, understanding the role of repolarization heterogeneity in arrhythmogenesis has clinical significance. This review aims to summarize experimental evidence on the genesis and electrocardiographic manifestations of repolarization dispersion, focusing specifically on electrophysiological markers associated with ventricular tachyarrhythmias in animal models of ischemia-reperfusion. Although the transmural repolarization gradient, along with apicobasal and interventricular gradients, was documented in intact hearts, its magnitude was significantly smaller than that of the inter-regional gradients, suggesting only a minor contribution to T wave genesis. Experimentally induced local myocardial ischemia increased global, apicobasal, and ischemia-border zone repolarization dispersions and was associated with prolongation of the Tpeak-Tend and corrected QT intervals, as well as increased T-wave amplitude dispersion. However, ventricular tachyarrhythmias were associated with increased duration of repolarization in the nonischemic zone rather than with repolarization dispersion, and this repolarization prolongation was reflected in the electrocardiogram as terminal T-wave inversion. In conclusion, ventricular arrhythmogenesis in ischemia-reperfusion is determined not only by spatial dispersion of repolarization but also by region-specific alterations in repolarization duration. ECG-derived markers, including morphological features, provide a noninvasive assessment of both repolarization dispersion and local repolarization duration abnormalities and therefore have the potential to improve risk stratification for malignant ventricular arrhythmias.

title: Case Report: Impella CP-protected percutaneous coronary intervention of the last remaining vessel-a LIMA-to-LAD graft-complicated by no-reflow and rescued with a drug-coated balloon.
summary: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the last remaining conduit in a patient with severely impaired left ventricular function is among the most hazardous procedures in contemporary interventional cardiology, as any interruption of flow essentially constitutes a global ischemic insult. We describe a 77-year-old man, a former heavy smoker with an 80-pack-year smoking history, who had undergone three-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) 22 years previously. His medical history also included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25-30%, and severe mitral regurgitation (MR). At presentation, he had Canadian Cardiovascular Society class III angina and New York Heart Association class III symptoms. The most recent coronary angiogram, performed 6 months earlier, demonstrated chronic total occlusion (CTO) of both saphenous vein grafts, in addition to CTO of all three native epicardial coronary arteries. Thus, the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft to the left anterior descending artery (LAD) represented the sole functional conduit, directly perfusing the LAD territory and supplying the right coronary and circumflex territories through primarily septal and epicardial collaterals, respectively. The LAD displayed two sequential severe stenoses (≥80% each), one at the distal LIMA-LAD anastomosis and another further distally in the native vessel. In accordance with current coronary revascularization guidelines, the Heart Team recommended evaluation by cardiac surgeons. Two independent cardiothoracic surgeons declined redo CABG as a viable therapeutic option. Complex and high-risk indicated PCI (CHIP) was therefore considered the only feasible revascularization strategy. Additional hemodynamic support with percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (pMCS) was deemed necessary. Residual MR and arrhythmic risk, including the potential indication for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), were planned to be reassessed 3 months after successful percutaneous revascularization. CHIP was performed under full hemodynamic support with a continuous-flow microaxial pump (Impella CP with SmartAssist) inserted via the left femoral artery, while coronary intervention was performed through the ipsilateral radial artery using a 6-F IMA guiding catheter. The lesions were successfully crossed with a workhorse wire, despite substantial technical difficulty and with the aid of a microcatheter; however, distal flow was immediately lost, and intracoronary nitroglycerin failed to restore it. Balloon angioplasty restored flow only partially, and a decision was made to proceed with stent implantation. However, stent delivery proved challenging, requiring a guide-extension catheter to be advanced deep into the LIMA body using the so-called 'inchworming technique.' Despite successful implantation of the first drug-eluting stent (DES) at the distal anastomotic lesion, a second DES could not be advanced to the more distal native LAD lesion, despite the use of multiple guidewires and supportive guiding-catheter strategies. Therefore, a drug-coated balloon (DCB) was used as a bailout strategy, immediately restoring TIMI grade 3 flow and leaving only a minor, non-flow-limiting type B dissection. Impella support was discontinued early because of access-related left lower-limb ischemia, and successful percutaneous hemostasis was achieved using a suture-based closure technique. Peak high-sensitivity troponin I, measured the following evening, was 10,800 pg/mL. The patient was discharged ambulatory on day 2 and remained asymptomatic at 3-month follow-up, when an ICD was implanted for primary prevention. This case illustrates the critical role of pMCS in maintaining hemodynamic stability when native coronary flow is lost during PCI of the last remaining conduit and highlights the value of DCB angioplasty as a bailout strategy when stent delivery is not feasible.

title: Endomyocardial biopsy after leadless pacemaker implantation in patient with suspected cardiac amyloidosis.
summary:
Leadless pacemakers (LPMs) are increasingly used especially in elderly patients; however, the safety of subsequent intracardiac procedures remains uncertain. We report a case of a 76-year-old man on maintenance hemodialysis with suspected cardiac amyloidosis who had previously undergone LPM implantation. Despite grade 3 uptake on technetium-99 m pyrophosphate scintigraphy, the presence of monoclonal protein and negative extracardiac biopsies necessitated endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) for definitive diagnosis. Preprocedural cardiac computed tomography demonstrated precise localization of the LPM near the right ventricular outflow tract. Based on these findings, EMB was safely performed via a femoral vein approach without device-related complications. Histopathology and gene test confirmed wild-type transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy. This case highlights the importance of individualized, imaging-guided procedural planning to safely perform EMB after LPM implantation.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE: Endomyocardial biopsy remains essential for definitive diagnosis and amyloid typing in patients with suspected transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy who have concomitant monoclonal protein, even when bone scintigraphy is strongly positive. In patients with a previously implanted leadless pacemaker, preprocedural imaging to evaluate the spatial relationship between the device and the intended biopsy site is critical for procedural safety.

title: Internal jugular vein approach facilitating second leadless pacemaker implantation after battery depletion.
summary:
Leadless pacemakers (LLPMs) have become an established treatment for bradyarrhythmias because they are associated with fewer lead-related complications and infections than transvenous pacemakers. However, when battery depletion occurs, implantation of a second device may be technically more challenging than the initial procedure because the available right ventricular (RV) implantation sites are limited by the existing device. We report a case of second LLPM implantation using the internal jugular vein (IJV) approach. A 92-year-old man with atrioventricular block had undergone Micra implantation 10 years earlier. The device battery was approaching depletion and implantation of a second LLPM was planned. Computed tomography revealed a narrow tricuspid valve and clockwise rotation of the RV. Because these anatomical features and the existing device could limit catheter maneuverability with the conventional femoral approach, the IJV approach was selected. The delivery catheter was advanced smoothly across the tricuspid valve and positioned superior to the existing device. The second Micra device was successfully deployed without mechanical interference with the initial device. No procedure-related complications occurred. The internal jugular approach may represent a useful alternative strategy for second LLPM implantation, particularly in patients with anatomical features or a previously implanted device limiting the available RV implantation site.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE: Implantation of a second leadless pacemaker (LLPM) may be more challenging than the initial procedure because of limited available implantation sites. LLPM implantation via the internal jugular vein (IJV) allows firm contact with the right ventricular septum and is associated with a lower risk of venous complications. The IJV approach represents a feasible alternative strategy for second Micra implantation.

title: NT-proBNP levels and arrhythmias in adolescents with chronic upper gastrointestinal diseases.
summary:
OBJECTIVE: To assess plasma N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels in adolescents with chronic upper gastrointestinal diseases and investigate their association with 24-hour Holter electrocardiographic findings.

METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 104 adolescents with endoscopically-verified chronic upper gastrointestinal diseases and 58 comparison adolescents without clinically-documented chronic gastrointestinal or cardiovascular disease. Both groups underwent 24-hour Holter electrocardiographic monitoring. NT-proBNP was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay in 60 patients and 28 controls. Receiver operating characteristic analysis explored the ability of this biomarker to identify positive Holter findings, defined as rhythm, conduction, or repolarization abnormalities exceeding age-related physiological limits or requiring further cardiological evaluation.

RESULTS: Positive Holter findings were observed in 71 patients (68.3%). Most findings were benign; potentially clinically significant abnormalities occurred in 11 patients (10.6% of all patients; 15.5% of those with positive Holter findings). Median NT-proBNP levels did not significantly differ between patients and controls but were higher in patients with cardiovascular complaints (53.0 42.5-85.0 versus 22.6 12.4-41.4 pg/mL; p=0.001) and positive Holter findings (50.0 32.2-70.5 versus 27.8 10.7-41.4 pg/mL; p<0.05). According to the receiver operating characteristic analysis for identifying positive Holter findings, we observed an area under the curve of 0.779 (95% confidence interval 95%CI: 0.726-0.833; p<0.001). An NT-proBNP cutoff value of ≥43.2 pg/mL showed 66.7% sensitivity and 90.9% specificity for identifying positive Holter findings.

CONCLUSIONS: Higher NT-proBNP levels were associated with positive Holter findings. Given the cross-sectional design and limited monitoring period, this association requires prospective validation.

title: Mapping the Research Landscape of Cardiac Magnetic Resonance in Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Bibliometric Analysis from 2016 to 2025.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure and sudden cardiac death, and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) has become an essential imaging modality for the diagnosis and risk assessment. However, the overall knowledge structure and research trends of CMR applications in DCM remain unclear.

METHOD: This study used bibliometric analysis to evaluate research on CMR in DCM from 2016 to 2025. Publications were searched from the Web of Science Core Collection database. CiteSpace and VOSviewer were used to analyze publication trends, citations, keywords, and keyword bursts.

RESULTS: A total of 1,296 articles were included in this study. JACC-Cardiovascular Imaging and Circulation ranked first and second, respectively, in terms of citations. The United States, England, and Italy were the three most highly cited countries, while Harvard Medical School, Mayo Clinic, and the University of Padua were the three most highly cited institutions. The 2023 ESC Guidelines were the most highly cited reference. Based on the keyword clustering analysis, four main clusters have been identified: myocardial fibrosis, quantitative mapping, inflammatory differential diagnosis, and arrhythmia risk assessment. Burst keyword analysis revealed an evolution from conventional functional and imaging assessment toward emerging topics involving machine learning, genetics, and arrhythmic risk stratification.

DISCUSSION: The findings suggest that CMR research in DCM has increasingly focused on tissue characterization and imaging-based risk evaluation. Imaging markers, such as late gadolinium enhancement and parametric mapping, are gradually being applied to identify patients with a higher risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Artificial intelligence will be used to develop a new kind of presentation for clinical data that is more accurate and user-friendly.

CONCLUSION: CMR is moving beyond traditional morphological assessment and is gradually being applied in risk stratification and personalized management of DCM. Based on the knowledge structure and research development in this area, this study provides a reference for future research and the clinical translation of emerging CMR techniques.

title: Emotional stress-induced hot phases in a patient with a desmoplakin-associated arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Desmoplakin (DSP) mutations are a common cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM), frequently presenting with recurrent myocarditis-like 'hot phases' that contribute to myocardial injury and increased arrhythmic risk.

CASE SUMMARY: A 40-year-old woman presented with acute chest pain and marked troponin elevation following emotional stress. Her history was notable for recurrent stress-related myocarditis episodes and a diagnosis of biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy due to a pathogenic DSP mutation. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrated diffuse myocardial oedema and a characteristic circumferential subepicardial ring-like pattern of late gadolinium enhancement, consistent with an active hot phase. Given the high-risk pathogenic DSP mutation with multiple high-risk features, including documented non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, frequent ventricular ectopy, and mild left ventricular disfunction (resulting in a calculated 5-year arrhythmic risk of 12% according to the novel DSP risk score)-and the presence of frequent hot phases recurrences and high burden of late gadolinium enhancement-a primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted after clinical stabilization. Medical therapy was optimized with β-blocker up-titration and low-dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor therapy targeting recurrent stress-related triggers. At follow-up, the patient reported sustained clinical well-being with no recurrence of hot phases or arrhythmic events.

CONCLUSION: This case exemplifies DSP-related arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy marked by recurrent, stress-triggered 'hot phases,' highlighting the pivotal interplay between inflammation and arrhythmic risk, and underscoring the need for refined, disease-specific risk stratification and targeted management strategies.

title: Inherited cardiovascular risk and its impact on healthspan and lifespan.
summary: Genetic disposition for cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major determinant of aging-related traits, such as healthspan, dementia, and frailty. While rare monogenic disorders provide important mechanistic insights, most CVDs and aging-related traits are driven by the cumulative effects of numerous common genetic variants, resulting in a polygenic risk architecture. Analyses of genes and pathways affected by these variants revealed significant correlations in the genetic architectures of CVD and aging, which appear to promote each other bidirectionally. Thus, CVD and aging share common genetic mechanisms, linking inherited cardiovascular risk to frailty, dementia, reduced healthspan, and shortened lifespan-and, conversely, explaining why aging is the strongest risk factor for atherosclerosis. Advances in genome-wide association studies have also enabled the construction of a polygenic risk score (PRS), which quantifies inherited CVD risk and facilitates early risk stratification beyond conventional clinical assessment. Importantly, individuals at high polygenic risk for CVD derive greater benefit from preventive strategies, which reduce their lifelong burden of CVD risk and ultimately promote healthy aging. Therefore, personalizing clinical risk assessment by integrating genetic testing for both CVD and aging-related traits may be of clinical importance. Specifically, lifestyle modification and preventive therapies based not only on conventional risk assessment, but also on polygenic risks may offer an individualized life-course approach for precision prevention, shifting cardiovascular care from reactive disease management toward the promotion of healthy aging.

title: Clinical, Imaging, and Genetic Characteristics of Adult Left Ventricular Noncompaction: A Single-Center Registry Study.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) is a heterogeneous cardiomyopathy characterized by excessive myocardial trabeculation and a variable clinical presentation. Although advances in multimodality imaging have improved diagnostic accuracy, prospective longitudinal risk stratification frameworks remain limited.

METHODS: This single-center registry study describes the baseline clinical, imaging, electrocardiographic, and genetic characteristics of adult patients with confirmed LVNC followed at a tertiary inherited cardiac conditions clinic, enrolled both prospectively and retrospectively. Baseline assessments included demographics, clinical history, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), electrocardiography, exercise stress testing, Holter monitoring, and genetic testing. This descriptive analysis does not include a formal time-to-event outcomes analysis, which is planned for future prospective follow-up of this cohort.

RESULTS: The cohort comprised 50 adults (34 women, 16 men; mean age at diagnosis 48.9 ± 13.4 years), enrolled prospectively (n = 38) and retrospectively (n = 12). Diagnosis was established by CMR in 80% of patients (n = 40), TTE in 18% (n = 9), and CT in 2% (n = 1). Presenting features included prior cardiac arrest (n = 3), syncope (n = 10), palpitations (n = 16), and a family history of sudden cardiac death (n = 9). Baseline TTE (available in 38 patients) showed a mean left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 51.8 ± 11.8%. CMR, available for 44 patients (88% of the cohort), confirmed LVNC in all cases, with the noncompacted-to-compacted ratio (NC:C) ranging from 2.8:1 to 6.3:1 (median 4.0:1); apical hypertrabeculation was universal, and lateral involvement was present in 72.7% (32/44) of CMR-imaged patients. Among 48 patients with electrocardiogram (ECG) data, T-wave abnormalities were present in 20.8% (10/48), left bundle branch block in 14.6% (7/48), and right bundle branch block in 6.3% (3/48). Genetic testing, performed in 32 of the 38 prospectively enrolled patients, identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 53% (17/32), most commonly in TTN (34%, 11/32); the remainder had variants of uncertain significance or no identified variant. Structured follow-up data were incomplete and variably attended, with follow-up 2 assessments available in 29 of 50 patients (58%); among those retested, LVEF remained preserved or only mildly reduced (mean 51.1% and 56% at follow-up 1 and 2, respectively).

CONCLUSIONS: This single-center registry demonstrates substantial phenotypic, morphologic, and genetic heterogeneity in adult LVNC, with CMR providing the most sensitive morphologic characterization and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified in approximately half of genetically tested patients. Since clinical outcome events and time-to-event analyses were not assessed in this baseline dataset, these findings are hypothesis-generating rather than prognostic. Thus, structured prospective follow-up of this cohort is needed to define arrhythmic and heart failure outcomes and to refine phenotype- and genotype-directed risk stratification.

CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT06024759 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06024759?cond=NCT06024759&viewType=Card&rank=1).

title: Non-Echocardiographic Evaluation of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
summary: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a heterogeneous genetic and phenotypic myocardial disease where diagnosis and risk stratification extend beyond the mere detection of left ventricular hypertrophy. While echocardiography is the first-line imaging modality, this approach often offers limited insights into disease etiology, biological activity, and natural history. Thus, several non-echocardiographic modalities have emerged as prominent components of contemporary HCM investigations. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides early, readily accessible insights into myocardial remodeling and arrhythmic risk. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging enhances phenotyping through detailed tissue characterization and fibrosis assessment, while nuclear imaging uniquely evaluates myocardial perfusion and microvascular injury. Plasma biomarkers and genetic testing offer valuable insights into disease activity and risk stratification for affected individuals and at-risk relatives, especially when combined with imaging findings. Therefore, this review summarizes current knowledge on non-echocardiographic approaches to HCM, highlighting the associated complementary strengths and the value of integrated multimodality assessment in improving disease phenotyping, prognostication, and management. Importantly, integrating these modalities improves risk stratification for sudden cardiac death, heart failure progression, and arrhythmias, guiding decisions on implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement and medical management. This approach supports more personalized, mechanism-based care in HCM.

title: Early recognition of PRKAG2 syndrome in an adolescent with a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy phenotype and ventricular pre-excitation: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: PRKAG2 syndrome is a rare glycogen-storage cardiomyopathy that can mimic sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). The diagnostic clue is not left ventricular hypertrophy alone, but the combination of hypertrophy with ventricular pre-excitation and conduction-system abnormalities. This pattern is clinically important because PRKAG2 syndrome differs from sarcomeric HCM in disease progression, arrhythmic risk, and long-term management.

CASE PRESENTATION: A 12-year-old boy presented with recurrent exertional chest tightness. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed ventricular pre-excitation, and echocardiography demonstrated asymmetric non-obstructive left ventricular hypertrophy. An external Holter report recorded sinus bradycardia and nocturnal pauses. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous PRKAG2 variant, NM_016203:c.1423A>G (p.Lys475Glu), classified as likely pathogenic. The available report from a clinically indicated invasive electrophysiological procedure documented persistent pre-excitation and localized the earliest antegrade ventricular activation to the right midseptal para-Hisian region. Catheter ablation was deferred because no tachyarrhythmia had been documented and ablation near the His bundle carried a substantial risk of atrioventricular block. During approximately 2 years of follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable, with persistent hypertrophy and no major arrhythmic or conduction events.

CONCLUSIONS: In adolescents with otherwise unexplained ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular pre-excitation should prompt consideration of PRKAG2 syndrome and other HCM phenocopies, even without a positive family history. Recognition of this combined structural and electrical phenotype may facilitate earlier genetic diagnosis and guide long-term rhythm surveillance. The mechanism of pre-excitation should be described only to the extent supported by the available electrocardiographic and procedural documentation.

title: Effect of clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential on long-term survival in patients with arrhythmias.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential(CHIP), defined by somatic mutations within hematopoietic clones, has emerged as a novel risk factor for cardiovascular disease. While cardiac arrhythmias are a major global health concern, the factors contributing to outcome variability remain unclear. The study aimed to investigate the association between CHIP and mortality in patients with arrhythmias.

METHODS: This study analyzed UK Biobank participants hospitalized with arrhythmias who had whole-exome sequencing data. Arrhythmia subtypes were classified using ICD-10 codes. Outcomes, including all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer-related mortality, were obtained from national registries. CHIP was defined as any CHIP as variant allele fraction(VAF) ≥ 2%, large CHIP as VAF ≥ 10%. Cox regression models adjusted for confounders were used.

RESULTS: Among 53,149 individuals (median age 69 years), 3,315 carried CHIP mutations. Both any and large CHIP were independently associated with higher mortality: adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for all-cause mortality were 1.26 (1.19-1.34) and 1.44 (1.33-1.55), respectively; for cardiovascular mortality, 1.14 (1.02-1.27) and 1.31 (1.14-1.52); and for cancer-related mortality, 1.36 (1.23-1.51) and 1.65 (1.45-1.87). Associations persisted across arrhythmia subtypes, with the strongest effects in ventricular arrhythmias. In gene-specific analyses, TET2, TP53 and spliceosome genes appeared to be the strongest deleterious genes for all-cause mortality [large TET2 CHIP: HR 1.63 (1.40-1.90); large TP53 CHIP: 1.83 (1.18-2.84); large spliceosome CHIP: HR 1.85 (1.32-2.59)].

CONCLUSIONS: CHIP is independently associated with increased mortality in patients with arrhythmias across different subtypes. These findings suggest that CHIP may serve as a potential prognostic marker and therapeutic target.
